entries.why_wrong: You're right that `sort()` mutates in place, but that's just how the method always works and isn't what breaks this output. The actual problem is what it compares: with no comparator, `sort()` turns 10, 2, 1 into strings and orders them as `'1'`, `'10'`, `'2'`.

Switching to a for loop would mean hand-rolling a whole sort algorithm, which isn't necessary here — `sort()` itself is the right tool. The real issue is that it's missing a comparator, so it compares stringified values instead of numbers; passing `(a, b) => a - b` fixes it without ditching `sort()`.

`sort()` doesn't throw based on array length; it happily runs on arrays of any size, including this three-element one, and returns a value without erroring. What actually goes wrong is silent: no comparator means elements are compared as strings, so `10` sorts before `2`.
